translations: He swung his axe again at the same spot. This time the cut was deeper, and Wu Gang kept his eyes fixed on the tree. As soon as the blade left the wood, the trunk began to heal; when he raised the axe again, all that remained was a strip of intact bark.
“Cut as you go?” he whispered.
A voice from the moonlit edge answered, “Seems so.”

Aman held the green bamboo slip, lifted his toes, and poked his head out from behind the thin mist of the cloud path. Moonlight fell like water on his slightly tense face, and the corner of the slip trembled as he unconsciously shook it, the page quivering as if it feared being startled by the wind.

He muttered to himself, “I noted ‘first round made progress’ earlier, but this osmanthus tree has closed again.” He traced a fine line with his finger on the slip, then abruptly erased that line, leaving only a few sloppy “—” marks.

At that moment, the wood chips from Wu Gang’s axe drifted down softly, landing on the stone steps of the Moon Palace and making a faint “splat-splat” sound. Aman looked up and saw Wu Gang standing beside the ancient osmanthus tree, brow furrowed, axe still raised as if he were about to split the whole tree in half.

Aman couldn’t help but mutter, “This tree really ‘self‑heals,’ chopping and closing again, like it drank moonlight potion.” After saying that, he unconsciously tapped the slip against a stone pillar, producing a crisp “dong” that added a beat to the silent cycle.

Wu Gang’s axe fell again, striking the trunk. Wood chips flew, but were instantly absorbed by the soft leaves, as if an invisible hand smoothed them away. Wu Gang’s brow tightened further, his voice a little urgent: “Why does the tree close itself every time I cut?”

Aman looked up, surprised but still keeping his recorder poised. “Record… record.” He flipped the slip to the next page and wrote a line: “Osmanthus tree’s wound closes with each cut, still in a loop.”

At that instant, the tree’s branches trembled gently, producing a soft “shush” as if silently mocking Wu Gang’s axe. Wu Gang heard it, raised an eyebrow, and laughed out loud: “This tree repairs itself better than me—truly a ‘playful little demon of the Moon Palace’!”

Aman pursed his lips and chuckled softly, “The words I record also ‘self‑repair.’ The freshly written ‘first round made progress’ got erased by me—hilarious.” He tapped the slip’s tip against the paper, producing a clear “ding,” as if adding a tiny footnote to the absurd loop.

The Moon Palace remained cold and quiet, only the tree’s branches quivering in the moonlight. Wu Gang’s axe fell again and again, yet never truly harmed the trunk. Aman lowered his head and kept recording, his pen scratching heavy lines on the slip, each word tinged with a faint lament for this endless punishment.
“When did you come?” Wu Gang finally looked up, his voice weary yet still stubborn.
Aman lifted his eyes, nodded gently, and said in a low, steady voice, “I just arrived, recording every iteration of this cycle.”
He gently closed the green bamboo slip; the pages glimmered faintly in the moonlight, as if reminding him that this record was also a lonely companion.
Wu Gang asked, “When did you come?”
“When you thought you could return in a few days.”
“Don’t remember that line.”
The young scribe lowered his head to look at the slip: “It’s already written. The tree will erase the axe marks, but my slip won’t.”

Wu Gang had no desire to argue. He switched to the other side, hoping to see if the original spot had any strange power. The new cut closed in the moonlight just as quickly, no difference in speed. He then chose a finer branch; after being struck, it bent but then instantly returned to its original shape.
The young scribe didn’t count this time, just noting that “trunk, side, and branches all recover.” He didn’t touch the axe or offer any spell, lest onlookers become the ones breaking the punishment.

Wu Gang didn’t believe a single tree could outpace his axe forever. He swung repeatedly, trying not to give the cuts time to close. The first few strikes did overlap, the tree dented inward; but the moment he switched hands, the moonlight filled in most of it. When his strength waned, the trunk returned to its original state.

He set the axe handle on the ground and, for the first time, seriously recalled the immortal teacher’s words: “Don’t rush to find another shortcut.” The tree’s nature was clearly part of the judgment; it couldn’t be solved with the old chopping experience.
Aman asked if they should record today’s result as “no progress.”
Wu Gang looked at the wood chips dispersing under the tree: “At least I know how it will recover.”
“Then that counts as the first truly finished lesson,” Aman said.

That statement was not a plea, nor did it lessen the task. Wu Gang still had to keep chopping; the condition for release remained to fell this indestructible osmanthus tree. Only now did he see clearly that the punishment wasn’t to complete a simple heavy task, but to make every hurried attempt to achieve results return to the starting point.
